Hostility

/hah-STIL-ih-tee/ - the stress falls on STIL · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Hostility means unfriendly or aggressive feeling or behavior toward someone.

The surveyors staking the pipeline route met open hostility at every farm gate: dogs loosed early, gates chained, and coffee offered to everyone but them.

Worked Example

The new head housekeeper felt it before she understood it: burnt toast on her tray alone, messages that arrived a day late, a staff room that went quiet when she entered. Nobody said a word against her. The hostility was in the pauses, the crossed arms, the thousand small services that somehow failed only her.

Hostility is the exact word because it names unfriendly or aggressive feeling or behavior toward someone — and it can be either: felt in an atmosphere or acted out in a hundred small slights. It needs no history and no reason; the staff barely knows her. The moment the unfriendliness is aimed and present, hostility is the name for it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

antagonism: Antagonism is active opposition between parties — the pushing-against of rivals, factions, or debaters, where each side works against the other. Hostility needs no contest at all: it is the unfriendly feeling or behavior itself, and a whole room can aim it at a newcomer who opposes no one. Antagonism implies a contest; hostility only implies the chill.

unfriendliness: Unfriendliness is the plain, milder word for the same chill — a neighbor who never waves, a reply kept short. Hostility is unfriendliness sharpened and aimed: the feeling or behavior points at someone, and they can feel it. All hostility is unfriendly, but plenty of unfriendliness never rises to hostility.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

warmth: open friendliness of feeling

friendliness: welcoming behavior toward someone

Where it sits · how far ill feeling turns to action — coldness → hostility → aggression

coldness vs. hostility: Coldness merely keeps warmth back; hostility points the unfriendliness at you and lets you feel it.

aggression vs. hostility: Aggression goes past hostility — the feeling has landed its first blow.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hostil

Root — hostil: enemy (Latin hostis, "enemy, stranger")

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: state of

Put it together

Put it together: Hostil- (from Latin hostis, "enemy, stranger") + -ity (state of) = the state of treating someone as an enemy. Rome used hostis for the stranger at the gate who might mean harm; hostility still names exactly that stance — enemy-feeling, whether it stays a mood or becomes an act.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin hostis ('enemy, stranger') built almost nothing else in English — its adjective twin hostile, which you may have met, is the whole family you'll ever meet. The friendly look-alike hospitality comes from a different Latin word, hospes ('guest, host'), which is why the two sound alike and mean opposites.

Word Choice

neutral

Hostility is the unfriendliness you can feel in the room right now — aimed at someone, shown in looks or acts. For hatred that has settled in for years between two parties, this unit's enmity is the word; for one person's deep, reasoned dislike, antipathy. And when the feeling finally throws something, it has crossed into aggression.
